record.passage:
Teacher's note, KG-B, Thursday
Naveen called out every answer in circle time before I finished the question, and at outdoor play he pushed Deepak to reach the red ball first. Deepak cried. Naveen looked surprised, as if his hands had moved before he knew.
No corner, no scolding. I sat with both boys: 'Hands stay still, then we talk.' We practised 'freeze like a statue' three times, laughing. Naveen said sorry and gave Deepak the ball.
In afternoon circle Naveen held up a star card instead of calling out. He waited four times.
Star card again next week.

qa.a: A star card, instead of calling out.

qa.q: What does Naveen's surprised look after pushing Deepak suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Naveen acted before thinking, as if his hands moved before he knew, and didn't mean to hurt Deepak.

qa.q: What choice did the teacher make after the push, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: The teacher skipped the corner and practised 'freeze like a statue' with both boys, teaching a calm stop without shame.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel after Naveen says sorry and hands over the ball?

row_description: A child hears others mock people with mental illness or a classmate with a difference, and learns that struggling is shameful. Adults who speak of feelings and health openly protect the child from hiding pain.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in an urban Indian setting (city flat, colony, market, school, office).

record.passage: In the colony park, the older boys pointed at the man who talked to himself near the gate. "Paagal! Paagal!" they chanted. Sunaina laughed too, then stopped. At night her own worries buzzed like mosquitoes and kept her awake. Would they call her paagal too? She decided never to tell anyone. Irfan Uncle from the second floor had heard the boys. That evening, watering his plants, he said, "That man's mind is unwell, the way a body gets unwell. It isn't funny, and it isn't his fault. I saw a doctor myself when my worries got too big." Sunaina twisted her frock. "Mine buzz at night," she whispered. Irfan Uncle put down the watering can. "Thank you for telling me. Let's go up and tell your Mummy together." They did, and Mummy hugged her and listened.

qa.q: What did the older boys chant?
qa.a: Paagal! Paagal!

qa.q: Why did Sunaina decide never to tell anyone about her night worries?
qa.a: After hearing the boys mock the man, she felt ashamed and feared they would call her paagal too.

qa.q: Which words from Irfan Uncle made it safe for Sunaina to speak?
qa.a: He said an unwell mind is like an unwell body, not funny and not anyone's fault, and that he too saw a doctor when his worries got too big.

qa.q: How might the man near the gate feel hearing the chant?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and ashamed, and less likely to reach out for help.

record.grounding: It shows a child learning from mockery that struggling is shameful, until an adult speaks openly about minds and health and she shares her own worries.

row_description: A child keeps checking where a parent is, asks repeatedly if they are loved and struggles with sleepovers. Fear of separation is real, and predictable goodbyes help more than dismissal.
recipe_text: Dialogue-heavy scene (mostly spoken lines, little narration): a family or home scene when the counterpart is family; otherwise set where that relationship naturally happens (class, office, team, street), still mostly dialogue.

record.passage:
"Amma, are you in the bathroom?"
"Yes, Lavanya. Still here."

row_description: A child may take words literally, find playground rules confusing and feel exhausted by school noise and effort to fit in. Clear, kind explanations help far more than punishment for misreading cues.

record.subtype: Social rules that are not obvious [Actor]
record.passage: My name's Dhruv and I sit next to Charu, so I saw most of it. At break she walked straight into the middle of the skipping rope while Mitali's group was counting. The rope smacked her leg and they all shouted, "You can't just barge in!" Charu stood very still. Then she asked, "Where is that written?" They thought she was being cheeky. I don't think she was. She looked like she really wanted to know. Last period she had her head on her desk and her fingers in her ears, though only the fan was going. Ma'am saw and didn't scold. Next morning a card was pinned by the door: Skipping - wait at the end and ask, "Can I jump in?" Charu read it twice. At break she waited at the end of the line.

qa.a: Wait at the end and ask, 'Can I jump in?'

qa.a: Dhruv thinks she genuinely wanted to know the rule, because she looked like she really wanted to know, not like she was being cheeky.

row_description: A young adult uses audio books, voice tools and extra time, and feels embarrassed at first to ask. Sharing the difference with tutors and employers usually earns understanding and shows real ability.

record.passage: 14 March Did it. Finally went to Jaya ma'am's office hours and said the words: "I have dyslexia. Could I get the reading list early, and extra time in the mid-sems?" My voice was shaking and I stared at her plant the whole time. I'd practised it for a week. She just nodded and said, "Of course. Thank you for telling me. Would audio versions help?" That's it. No face. No sigh. All this semester I've been listening to the chapters on my phone at double speed on the bus and dictating notes with the voice tool. I thought using them was cheating. It isn't. It's how I read. Got back my essay today too: "Sharp argument." Pinned it above the desk. - Santosh

qa.a: The reading list early and extra time in the mid-sems.

row_description: A child may seem cranky, tired, tearful or lose interest in play, and complain of aches. Children often cannot say I feel low, so behaviour shows it, and a lasting change deserves attention.
recipe_text: An elder (grandparent, uncle, senior colleague) tells the story to a younger person as a memory or example, in their voice.

record.passage: "Suraj, you're teaching Class 4 now, so listen to your old Vaibhav Chacha for a minute. Years ago I had a boy in my class, bright as a lamp. Around Diwali he changed. He snapped at his friends over nothing. He put his head on the desk every afternoon. He stopped playing kabaddi, which he used to love, and every week he said his stomach hurt. The other teachers said, 'Cranky phase. He'll grow out of it.' But it didn't pass. Weeks, then two months. One day I asked him gently, 'What's it like inside, these days?' He said, 'Grey, Sir.' Just that. Grey. I called his parents that same evening, and they took him to a doctor who helped. Children don't say 'I feel low,' Suraj. They show it. Watch for the change that stays."

qa.q: What game did the boy stop playing?
qa.a: Kabaddi, which he used to love.

qa.q: What did the boy's answer 'Grey, Sir' reveal about how he felt?
qa.a: It revealed that he felt low and flat inside, even though he had only shown it as crankiness and tiredness.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav Chacha advise Suraj to watch for?
qa.a: A change in a child that stays, because children show low mood through behaviour instead of saying it.

qa.q: How did the other teachers see the boy's behaviour, and why was that risky?
qa.a: They saw a cranky phase he'd grow out of, which could have left his lasting sadness unnoticed.

record.grounding: An elder recalls a child whose low mood showed as crankiness, tiredness, lost interest in play and stomach aches, and a lasting change that got attention.

record.passage:
Monday. At the new playgroup, four-year-old Lakshmi stood pressed against her father's knees. When the teacher asked her name, she whispered "Lakshmi" into Thomas's shirt. Thomas didn't push. They sat on the bench and watched the sand tray.
Wednesday. Lakshmi let go of his hand to stand near the sand tray. A boy offered her a spade and she shook her head, but she kept watching him.
Friday. Lakshmi took the spade. By the end of the morning she was filling buckets beside the same boy, humming. At home she told her father, "He's my friend. His name is Omar."

row_description: A wise adult shares their own experience only when comfortable, treats mental health like physical health and supports others without pity. Each respectful conversation makes it easier for the next person to ask for help.
recipe_text: An observer's account: a neighbour, sibling, classmate or colleague describes what they saw, without knowing the protagonist's inner state for sure.

record.passage: I'm Ganga. I sit two desks from Salma at the accounts office, and I've watched her do something I didn't know was possible. When Mohan said he was leaving early for physio, Salma said, just as easily, "I'm off at five too, therapy day." No drama. When Hemant pushed, "Therapy for what?", she smiled and said, "That's mine to keep, but it helps." I think it cost her something, though I can't be sure. Last month our new trainee, Varsha, cried in the washroom after a bad review. Salma didn't say "poor thing". She sat down beside her and said, "Rough day. Want some water? If it keeps feeling heavy, our company counsellor is good." Since then, two people have mentioned their own counselling at lunch as if it were a dentist visit. I don't know if Salma planned that. I just know the room feels different.

qa.q: What did Salma say when Hemant asked "Therapy for what?"
qa.a: That's mine to keep, but it helps.

qa.q: What does Ganga think about how Salma felt when speaking openly?
qa.a: Ganga thinks it may have cost Salma some nerve or discomfort, though Ganga can't be sure.

qa.q: Which choices in the washroom supported Varsha without pity?
qa.a: Salma sat beside her, called it a rough day, offered water and mentioned the company counsellor, without saying "poor thing".

qa.q: Why might Varsha remember Salma's response differently from a "poor thing"?
qa.a: A "poor thing" might have made Varsha feel pitied and small; Salma's calm, ordinary words let it feel like a normal rough day with help available.

record.grounding: It shows a young woman at work who speaks of therapy as plainly as physio, keeps details private, supports a trainee without pity, and makes it easier for others to talk.

record.passage: In the colony sandpit, Ojas digs his own road right beside Rehana's castle, never touching it. He doesn't look at her, but he stays. "The blue bus goes from the market to the beach," he says, "and it has two doors, and the back door squeaks." Then he names every stop, in order, twice. Rehana pats sand onto her tower and listens. When her castle is done, Ojas quietly drives his toy bus right up to its gate and parks it there. "Bus stop," he says. Rehana grins. "Okay. My castle has a bus stop now."

qa.a: Right up to the gate of Rehana's castle.

row_description: A boy told not to cry hides sadness and a girl told to be quiet hides ambition. Learned rules shape which traits feel safe, and adults who widen the range help teenagers become fuller selves.
recipe_text: An elder (grandparent, uncle, senior colleague) tells the story to a younger person as a memory or example, in their voice.

record.passage:
Harsha, you think I was always this old man who cries at films? At fifteen I was told, 'Men don't cry, Yusuf.' When my elder brother left for work in the Gulf and I didn't know when I'd see him again, I went behind the well and bit my sleeve so no one would hear.
My Urdu teacher, Masterji, found me there. He didn't laugh. He sat down and said, 'Tears are not a woman's thing or a man's thing. They are a heart's thing.' Then he cried a little too, about his own son far away.
I have never forgotten that. So when your mother says you should keep quiet about becoming a pilot, I'll tell you what Masterji told me: the heart doesn't care about these rules. Say it out loud. I'll be the first to clap.

qa.q: Where did Yusuf go to cry when his brother left?
qa.a: Behind the well, biting his sleeve so no one would hear.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf hide his tears at fifteen?
qa.a: He had been told 'Men don't cry', so he felt sadness was not safe to show.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Yusuf saw crying?
qa.a: Masterji finding him, not laughing, saying tears are a heart's thing and then crying too, widened what felt allowed.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel hearing Yusuf promise to be the first to clap?
qa.a: Harsha may feel encouraged and less alone in the pilot dream, with an adult openly on Harsha's side.

record.grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a boy taught not to cry who hid his sadness, and adults who widen which feelings and ambitions feel safe.

recipe_text: A note written by an adult who watched: caregiver, teacher, counsellor, coach or supervisor (their observations, plus what they did next).

record.passage:
Project mentor's note, Mehak, Class 10 science exhibition.
Dhruv has taken over his group's solar-car model completely. He assigns every task, redoes wiring others have done and says "Just let me" a lot. When Anjali tried to paint the chassis, he took the brush from her. Today I asked him to step back for one hour while the group chose the colour scheme. He paced and kept glancing over, clearly anxious. Afterwards he admitted, "I'm scared it'll fail and it'll be my fault." That helped me understand him. His teammates have gone very quiet this week.
Next step: each member now owns one part, and Dhruv leads only the testing. We check in on Friday.

qa.a: He took the brush from her when she tried to paint the chassis.

qa.a: They had gone quiet and probably felt unheard, but owning their own parts may help them feel included again.

row_description: A teenager sets clear goals, tracks results and feels restless without a target. Drive brings progress, but success can become the only measure of worth if rest and relationships are neglected.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative in a rural or small-town Indian setting (village, farm, kasba, local bus, temple fair, small shop).

record.passage:
Zeenat's notebook had a column for every morning since January: distance, time, how she felt. On the dirt road past the sugarcane fields, she ran before the azaan finished and was back before her brothers woke.
The district meet was over now. She'd won silver. For two days she felt light. By the third she was pacing the courtyard, tapping her fingers, asking Abbu when the state trials were.
'Beta, rest a week,' he said.
'A week is too long.'
That evening her cousin Mehak came over with henna cones for Friday's wedding. 'You'll come to the mehendi, na? You missed my engagement for practice.'
Zeenat opened her mouth to say she had a long run that night. Then she saw Mehak's face, hopeful and a little braced.
'I'll come,' she said, and closed the notebook.

qa.q: What did Zeenat record in her notebook each morning?
qa.a: Distance, time and how she felt.

qa.q: Why was Zeenat pacing the courtyard by the third day?
qa.a: Without a new target she felt restless and bored, already hungry for the state trials.

qa.q: What choice did Zeenat make when Mehak asked about the mehendi, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She chose to go instead of doing a long run, making room for a relationship that her training had been crowding out.

qa.q: How does Mehak seem to feel about Zeenat's training?
qa.a: Mehak seems hopeful but braced for another no, since Zeenat already missed the engagement for practice.

record.grounding: Shows a teenager who tracks goals and feels restless without a target, and a moment where she makes room for a relationship her drive had been crowding out.

row_description: A person in overwhelming emotional pain may harm themselves to feel relief or numbness, then feel shame. Behind it is suffering that needs care, not punishment, and help from a professional and trusted people.
recipe_text: First-person reflective account by the protagonist, looking back a little (for 7-12 keep it simple and short).

record.subtype: Hurting as a way to cope with pain [Actor]
record.passage: I'm Sabina, and I'm writing this a year on. Last winter my job ended and my grandmother fell ill in the same month. The pain felt too big for one body. I started hurting myself when it got unbearable, because for a little while afterwards I felt quiet and numb. Then shame would flood in, and I'd hide it under long sleeves and jokes. Ojas, who shared my desk at the office, noticed me flinch when he bumped my arm. He didn't lecture or look disgusted. He said, "Whatever's going on, you don't deserve to be punished for it. Can I help you find someone to talk to?" That week I saw a doctor and began seeing a psychologist. Some nights the urge still comes. Now I call Ojas or my sister instead, and we talk until it passes.

qa.q: What happened to Sabina last winter?
qa.a: Sabina's job ended and Sabina's grandmother fell ill in the same month.

qa.q: Why did Sabina hide it under long sleeves and jokes?
qa.a: Shame flooded in afterwards, so Sabina was afraid of being judged if anyone saw.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Sabina?
qa.a: Ojas responded without disgust and offered to help find someone to talk to; that week Sabina saw a doctor and began seeing a psychologist.

qa.q: What might Ojas have felt when Sabina flinched?
qa.a: Ojas probably felt worried and unsure, yet chose gentle words about not deserving punishment so Sabina could accept help.

record.grounding: It shows a young adult who hurt themselves for numb relief and felt shame, and found care through a desk mate's non-judging words, a doctor and a psychologist.

row_description: A child startles at loud sounds, has nightmares or plays out scary scenes again and again, or shuts down when reminded. Safety, routine and trusted adults help, and a child specialist is worth seeing.
recipe_text: Third-person narrative set outside India (any country), ordinary everyday detail.

record.passage: Since the car crash in the spring, Emeka, eight, hadn't been the same. Every afternoon in their London flat he crashed two toy cars together, over and over, making the sound of screeching brakes. At night he woke calling out. When a bus braked hard outside the school gate, he froze on the pavement and couldn't answer when his friend Bao said his name. Bao didn't pull him or laugh. He stood right next to Emeka and waited, holding out a sweet, until Emeka blinked and took it. Emeka's mum kept every day the same: the same route to school, the same story at bedtime, the same night light. His teacher knew to warn him before fire drills. And every Thursday Emeka and his mum went to see a child specialist, who played with him and listened.

qa.q: What did Bao hold out to Emeka at the school gate?
qa.a: A sweet.

qa.q: What does Emeka freezing on the pavement suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests the sound of braking brought the crash back, and he was frightened and shut down.

qa.q: Which choices by the adults around Emeka help him feel safe?
qa.a: His mum keeps a steady routine, his teacher warns him before fire drills, and he sees a child specialist every week.

qa.q: How might Bao have felt when Emeka didn't answer?
qa.a: Bao may have been worried or confused, but stayed calm and waited beside Emeka.

record.grounding: It shows a child who replays a frightening event in play, has nightmares and shuts down at reminders, helped by safety, routine, trusted adults and a child specialist.

row_description: A parent or relative may think the child is picky or dramatic about clothes or food. Listening, believing the child and trying small adjustments reduces daily battles.

record.subtype: Family member misreading it as fussiness [Receiver]
record.passage: "Abhinav, sit. You say your little one is fussy with food? Let me tell you about my Tashi. When he was nine, he would not eat dal if there was one lump in it. Rice touching the vegetables? He'd push the plate away and cry. I thought, this boy is spoilt. My mother-in-law said the same. Every dinner was a war. One night he whispered, 'Ama-la, the lumps feel like stones in my mouth. It makes me want to be sick.' Stones, Abhinav. He wasn't being clever. He was telling me. So I strained his dal smooth and gave him a plate with little walls. Just that. The wars stopped. Before you call her fussy, ask her what the food feels like. Then believe her." Dolma poured him more tea.

qa.q: What did Tashi say the lumps felt like?
qa.a: Like stones in his mouth.

qa.q: What did Dolma realise when Tashi whispered about the lumps?
qa.a: She realised he wasn't being clever or spoilt; he was honestly telling her how the food felt.

qa.q: What advice does Dolma give Abhinav about his little one?
qa.a: To ask the child what the food feels like and believe the answer before calling her fussy.

qa.q: What was dinner like for Tashi before Dolma listened?
qa.a: It was a daily war where he felt upset and was called spoilt, with food that felt like stones.

record.grounding: An elder recalls thinking her son was picky about food, then listening, believing him and making small adjustments that ended the daily battles.

At dinner he talked for twenty minutes about the play.

qa.a: He sat on the clubhouse steps for twenty minutes, watching.

record.passage:
Fifteen minutes before the annual day show, the stage lights failed, and everyone backstage was shouting. Gopika stood in a corner holding the host's script she had written herself. She'd wanted to host, but her aunt always said girls who push forward look proud, so she had let Arnav take it.
Farhan sat on a crate, jaw tight. His grandfather had gone into hospital that morning, and when his eyes filled at breakfast, his uncle had said, 'Be a man.'
Mrs Iyer, torch in hand, saw them both. To Farhan she said quietly, 'You're allowed to be worried. Sit with me a minute.' He let a few tears fall, and his shoulders dropped.
Then she handed Gopika the torch. 'Arnav's frozen. You know this script best. Will you open the show?'
Gopika hesitated, then stepped out.

qa.q: Why had Gopika let Arnav host?
qa.a: Her aunt always said girls who push forward look proud.

qa.q: What does Farhan's tight jaw suggest he was holding in?
qa.a: It suggests he was holding back worry and sadness about his grandfather after being told to 'be a man'.

Shift supervisor's note, Friday, café team
Two of my trainees handled today's order mix-up very differently. A table of eight got the wrong food because the order slip was smudged in the rain and the printer was down.

At the end of the day, while I was packing test papers, Divyansh hovered at my desk. "Sir, can I talk to you? It's kind of serious." My first instinct was to say, "Tomorrow, I'm late." I'm glad I didn't. He told me he hasn't slept properly for weeks, that his chest tightens every morning at the school gate, and that he's scared his parents will think he's making excuses for his marks. I put the papers down and said, "Thank you for telling me. That took courage." I gave him no speech about studying harder.
What I did next: I walked him to the school counsellor's room before she left, and with his permission I phoned his mother, who came in that evening. As he left, Divyansh asked if he could come back to me if it got worse. I said yes. I think he will.

record.passage: At the college canteen, Chandrika lined up her highlighters by colour and announced, "Sorry, I'm so OCD." Everyone laughed. Then someone said the new maths lecturer was "totally mental" for springing a surprise test, and the laughter got louder. Sumit noticed Faisal, at the end of the table, go very still and stare into his tea. Sumit took a breath. "Can I say something without being annoying? People who actually live with OCD describe it as exhausting, not neat pens. And calling the lecturer 'mental', maybe let's not." Chandrika went red. "Oh. I didn't think. Sorry." The table was awkward for a second, then someone asked about the test and the talk moved on. That evening Faisal messaged Sumit: "Thanks for saying that. I've been seeing a counsellor for a while. I never felt I could say it in that group."
